text: With no mapping configured at all, the Copy activity maps source data to sink by column name, case-sensitively. If the sink doesn't exist yet, the source's own field names simply become the sink's names. This default behavior genuinely supports schema drift — if the source's columns change from one run to the next, default mapping just picks up whatever the source actually returns each time, with no pipeline change required at all.

Sometimes that isn't enough, though. Explicit mapping handles copying only part of the source data, renaming columns along the way, or reshaping data between fundamentally different structures. Select Import schemas to bring in both sides, then map exactly what you actually need — exclude or delete the rest. This is also how you handle a source with no header row at all, mapping by column position instead of by name.

Explicit mapping goes further still. Copying from a hierarchical source — Cosmos DB, MongoDB, a REST API — into a flat, tabular sink, you can flatten nested arrays directly inside the mapping itself. Select the array to iterate over as the Collection reference, and the service cross-applies it, turning one single nested object into multiple flat rows automatically.

Choosing default mapping when you genuinely need renamed or filtered columns just means the wrong data lands in the sink. Choosing explicit mapping when the source schema actually changes often means a pipeline that breaks the moment someone adds a column upstream. Next: two activities that read data without necessarily moving anything at all — Lookup and Stored Procedure.
